questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: A famous octopus that predicted the results of football matches
questions.why: Neil says the programme is about the octopus, 'which apparently is a pretty clever animal'.

questions.q: What does Catherine first think a cephalopod is?
questions.why: She jokes 'It's a new kind of ipod, isn't it?'

questions.q: What is Catherine's opinion of Paul the octopus?
options: He really could see the future
He was the cleverest octopus that has ever lived in a zoo
He wasn't psychic; it was a publicity stunt
questions.why: She says 'I don't think he was really psychic' and it was a publicity stunt by the zoo.

options: He got only 6 out of 14 matches right
questions.why: Neil says he correctly predicted the result of 12 matches out of 14.

questions.q: According to Peter Godfrey-Smith, when did our common ancestor with the octopus live?
options: About 60 million years ago, with the dinosaurs
questions.why: He says it lived 'about 600 million years ago or actually even a bit longer'.

questions.q: Why does Godfrey-Smith compare the octopus's nervous system with vertebrates'?
options: To show it is large, which is a sign of intelligence
To show that octopuses have a backbone
To explain why octopuses are so small
To say octopuses are closely related to humans
questions.why: He says it's in a range comparable to vertebrates, and Neil says a large nervous system is a sign of intelligence.

questions.q: Which parts of the octopus's world are easy for us to understand?
questions.why: He says they're very visual and taste-oriented animals, and 'those things make sense to us'.

questions.q: Why is it hard for us to think about the octopus, according to Godfrey-Smith?
options: It lives too deep in the sea
It is too small to study
It has no senses that work in the same way as ours
It has no hard parts and can change shape
questions.why: He says the absence of hard parts and the protean nature of the body make it hard to think about.
